blogs.title: Exemption 7(A) as a Perpetual Shield? The D.C. Circuit Blesses 'Ongoing Investigations' a Decade On
blogs.description: The court affirms broad deference to the FBI’s invocation of Exemption 7(A) based on an investigation asserted to be ongoing for years, relying on CREW and Juarez to allow agency attestations to suffice. The post examines the legal significance of requiring time-stamped updates (Hardy to Bender) yet accepting terse confirmations, and questions how long 'ongoing' can persist before staleness undermines the exemption.

blogs.title: Behind Closed Doors: Ex Parte Declarations, FOIA, and the Limits of Adversarial Testing
blogs.description: The panel leans heavily on ex parte, sealed declarations to sustain both 7(A) and segregability, citing Perioperative Services for the necessity of such submissions in national security cases. This post explores the tension between transparency and secrecy, the practical effect of a requester’s failure to object, and what process courts should require to test ex parte claims without revealing the very information at issue.

blogs.title: Segregability in the Shadow of National Security: How 10,750 Pages Yielded 'No Meaningful Information'
blogs.description: Relying on Mead’s 'inextricably intertwined' concept, the court agreed that no reasonably segregable, meaningful material could be released across thousands of pages and 80 CDs. The post analyzes how national-security justifications and mosaic concerns can effectively swallow segregability, and proposes strategies for courts and requesters to cabin overbroad 'line-by-line interspersion' claims.

blogs.title: What Counts as a 'Proceeding' Under 7(A)? The Elastic Standard of 'Pending or Reasonably Anticipated'
blogs.description: Building on CREW, the opinion treats ongoing criminal investigations as qualifying 'proceedings' and accepts agency attestations of their existence and vulnerability to interference. This post probes the 'concrete prospective law enforcement proceeding' requirement, the interplay with FOIA’s foreseeable-harm standard, and whether the decision further dilutes the evidentiary showing agencies must make to invoke 7(A).

blogs.title: Requester Neutrality Meets Real-World Context: Using Farahi’s Immigration Record to Prove Law-Enforcement Purpose
blogs.description: Although FOIA is requester-neutral, the court relied on Farahi’s concessions and allegations from his immigration case to substantiate a law-enforcement nexus. This post evaluates the doctrinal soundness of importing facts from parallel proceedings to satisfy Pratt/Campbell’s 'rational nexus' test and considers the risks of reaffirming exemptions through allegations the requester cannot effectively contest in FOIA litigation.

blogs.title: Practice Pointers After Farahi: Building and Challenging Category-Based Withholdings
blogs.description: The panel deems challenges to the FBI’s categories forfeited for lack of specificity, while blessing category-based 7(A) withholdings supported by declarations. This practitioner-focused post distills lessons on preserving objections, forcing detail in Vaughn submissions, seeking sampling or in camera review, and demanding updated declarations when a case grows stale.

blogs.title: FOIA at the National-Security/Immigration Crossroads
blogs.description: Farahi’s FOIA case ran parallel to long-running removal proceedings where DHS relied on FBI counterterrorism evidence. This post situates the decision in the broader landscape where FOIA functions as a shadow discovery tool, assesses how 7(A) can foreclose access even to information used against a noncitizen in civil enforcement, and explores due-process-adjacent pressures the opinion sidesteps.

blogs.title: Deference Endures: Farahi in the Post-9/11 FOIA Canon
blogs.description: Placed alongside CNSS, Campbell, and more recent cases like Perioperative Services and Reps. Comm., the opinion underscores the D.C. Circuit’s continued deference to executive judgments in national-security FOIA disputes. This post tracks the trend lines, weighs the effect of DOJ’s pro-disclosure guidance against entrenched doctrine, and considers whether legislative or doctrinal reform is needed to recalibrate Exemption 7(A).
